title: Design a Contact Form
brief: A busy site has a contact form. A visitor writes a message and presses send, and the site must email it to its staff. Sending email goes through an outside email provider, which takes a moment and sometimes fails. The visitor should not have to wait for the email to go, and every message must reach the staff once: not lost, and not sent twice. Now and then a campaign sends a surge of messages.
constraints: The form must respond within 100 ms, however long the email takes
About 200 messages per second on a normal day, and up to about 5 times that during a campaign
Every message must be delivered once: not lost, and not sent twice, even if the provider fails and the send is tried again
The form keeps accepting messages when the email provider is down

capabilities.label: Accept a message
capabilities.hint: Check the message and record that it arrived.

capabilities.label: Deliver the message by email
capabilities.hint: Hand the message to the email provider. Select the block that runs it and tick it under Hosts. A message must not be sent twice.

scenarios.title: Normal day
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Follow one message from the visitor to the staff's inbox. At which point does the visitor stop waiting?
scenarios.debrief: The visitor only needs to wait until the message is safely accepted. Everything after that can happen later.

scenarios.title: A campaign (5x)
scenarios.description: A campaign sends five times the usual messages for a while.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Five times as many messages arrive. Which part of your design has to keep up with them, and which part can fall behind for a while?
scenarios.debrief: Accepting a message is quick and cheap, so it keeps up. The slower delivery work needs enough workers to keep up with what arrives, or the messages queue up.

scenarios.title: The email provider stops answering
scenarios.description: The outside email provider is unavailable.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: The provider is down. What does a visitor see when they press send, and what happens to the message?
scenarios.debrief: If delivery is part of the request, the visitor's form fails with the provider. If delivery happens later, the form still works and the messages wait to be sent.

requirements.text: The form responds within the latency target on a normal day
The form copes with a campaign
Messages are still accepted when the email provider is down
Accepting a message does not wait for it to be delivered
Something delivers each message by email
The design explains what happens to a message when the provider fails, and how a retry avoids sending it twice

rubric: The form accepts and records the message quickly, and the visitor does not wait for the email to be sent.
Delivery happens later, from a list of waiting messages, by workers that call the email provider.
If the provider fails, the message waits and delivery is tried again; the design says so.
A retry cannot send the same message twice: delivery is idempotent, and the design says how.
The workers are sized to keep up with a campaign, and delivery trouble does not stop messages being accepted.

reference.summary: Accept the message quickly and put it on a queue, and let idempotent workers deliver it through the provider, retrying if it fails.
design: User, then a Server with two replicas running 'Accept a message'.
The Server hands each message to a Queue over an async connection, and Workers read the Queue.
The Workers run 'Deliver the message by email', with idempotent processing on and retries enabled, and call a Third-party API set to Email / SMS.
tradeoffs: The visitor's wait no longer depends on the provider, but a message is delivered a little later than it was accepted.
Idempotent workers make a retry safe, at the cost of a check for every message.
The queue and workers are more blocks to pay for; the queue only holds work, it does not make it disappear, so the workers must still keep up.
